questions.question: What is the go.sum file and why is it needed?
questions.title: Go Sum
questions.direct_answer: Cryptographic hashes of every dependency's content. go test/build verifies downloaded modules against go.sum before use — supply-chain integrity. Commit it alongside go.mod.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Cryptographic hashes of every dependency's content. go test/build verifies downloaded modules against go.sum before use — supply-chain integrity. Commit it alongside go.mod.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The file, verified after our tidy:
```
github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0 h1:NIvJDL...
```

Each line: module, version, and three hash fields (the module directory content, the .mod file, and the go.mod file). After download, the hashes are verified — a corrupted or tampered dependency fails the build.

What go.sum IS: an integrity verification list — 'these are the exact bytes we downloaded.' NOT a lock file: it doesn't select versions (go.mod's requires do that). Both exist to make builds reproducible.

Why both files: go.mod selects the version; go.sum verifies the content. A lock file conflates both; Go separates selection from verification — and the same version can appear in different builds' go.sums with the same hashes (verification) while go.mod's selection is per-module.

The supply-chain story: a compromised proxy or a deleted-and-republished tag would serve different bytes for the same version — go.sum catches the difference. Without it, 'v1.6.0' could be anything.

The discipline: commit both go.mod and go.sum. If go.sum is missing/empty (fresh clone), go mod download or go mod tidy recreates it — and CI verifies.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    D[download module v1.6.0] --> H[hash the bytes]
    H --> CMP{== go.sum hash?}
    CMP -->|yes| OK[build proceeds]
    CMP -->|no| FAIL[security error — tampering]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The hash types: go.sum records hashes for the module's source directory (the extracted zip), the .mod file, and the go.mod file — each is verified against the downloaded artifact. The algorithm is SHA-256, and the format is the same as go.sum's snapshot format.

The verification flow: on import, the module proxy/cache is consulted → the version is downloaded → its content is hashed → compared to go.sum → mismatch aborts with a security error. Clean, deterministic, and the failure names the exact module/version that changed.

The -mod=mod vs -mod=readonly flag story: -mod=readonly (the default for builds) refuses to update go.mod/go.sum (fails if they'd change — the reproducibility guarantee); -mod=mod (go get/tidy) updates them. This is why `go build` errors when go.sum is missing — it won't silently add the verification entries.
